https://www.telegraph.co.uk/cricket/2023.title: Australia look beaten – only the rain can save them from England
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/cricket/2023.text:
This has been a brutal few days to wear a Baggy Green. Only once before in Test history had they conceded runs at more than the 5.49 an over that England smashed here. This was England’s first total at home of more than 500 in an Ashes Test since 1985; which is great credit to their heart and fight when you consider they were down and out in the series not that long ago.
Pat Cummins and Mitchell Starc did not bowl a single maiden in 48 overs and his 1-129 was the Australia captain’s worst ever Test figures. Cummins was battered by England, losing control in the field and constantly chasing the game with his tactics. The last man stand between James Anderson and Bairstow of 66 in 8.1 overs was ruthless bossing of the alpha males of Test cricket.
Bairstow’s bullying delayed England’s declaration and there was a touch of sentiment as Ben Stokes held back and enjoyed the view as every Australia fielder was posted on the boundary in damage limitation mode.
Bairstow has endured a tough few weeks but a stunning catch in the first innings soothed his nerves and he transferred it into his batting. The strut was back, along with the thousand-yard stare. The situation, coming in at 437 for five with his team on top, was tailor made for him to pummel some point-proving runs. He dumped the Aussie quicks over the boundary rope as easily as picking up a Just Stop Oil protester.
When Anderson came in, Bairstow was on 49 and looking up at the balcony expecting the declaration. A switch was flicked. As Australia spread the field, he simply put the ball over the rope making the biggest square boundaries in England irrelevant. He swatted flat sixes off Starc and Josh Hazlewood, and suddenly a hundred became a possibility.
Stokes mouthed “wow that’s massive” and banged on the dressing room window as Bairstow’s six off Cummins sailed high into the stands. Anderson cannily scampered byes to the keeper, Alex Carey, so Bairstow could pinch the strike. Bairstow loved it as the man who stumped him so controversially at Lord’s kept missing the stumps. Bairstow added to the theatre with elaborate taps in his crease and checks with the umpire that the ball was dead.
The crowd bayed for a hundred. On 98 Bairstow smacked one down to long off and set off for two and a huge roar turned to a groan as he had to settle for one, turning Anderson back. He stood helpless as Anderson tried to clip Green to leg but was lbw; the inevitable review was futile. Bairstow became only the second batsman to finish unbeaten on 99 in an Ashes Test, and it was the second time in his career he had fallen one short of a hundred, but he still wore a massive smile as he walked off.
The declaration could have come sooner and perhaps England will regret using up those overs but it was not as if they were patting the ball around. This was blistering cricket and it entertained the sell out crowd, which is part of England’s remit these days. It also lifted Bairstow, who is buzzing now and this ‘confidence cricketer’ will go to the Oval next week for what should be a decider, feeling like a world beater. That could reap dividends.
He vindicated the faith in him from the selectors, the second to do so this week after Zak Crawley. Wood has proved the value of holding him back until he was fully fit and Chris Woakes is enjoying this renaissance, with Australians believing he has been the difference since coming back to the side.
Anderson was tidy, Moeen Ali a bit wasteful and Stuart Broad struggled with his line with the new ball. The best bowlers were Chris Woakes and Wood. Woakes ploughed a consistent line and length making it nip off the surface while Wood’s pace pushed Australians on to the back foot.
Wood struck with his second ball of the innings, Usman Khawaja wafting away from his body. David Warner succumbed to a tough examination of his off stump by Woakes, playing on for 28. Steve Smith feathered a Wood bouncer down the leg side and Travis Head was well and truly worked over by the short ball. England have persevered with the tactic to Head and he has often survived it well enough, but this time he found himself in a tangle to a Wood bumper and fended a catch to gully.
The pitch is still flat, despite the cracks and the odd ball shooting through, so England will have to work for the remaining wickets but the biggest obstacle to victory is something they cannot control. Look up not down they say when assessing conditions at England’s northern Test grounds. Everyone’s eyes will be on the heavens for the next two days.
I don’t have a view.
On his form behind the stumps
I haven’t kept wicket for three years. I have nine pins, a plate and a wire running through my ankle. I’ve had nine months out. It’s part and parcel of it. I’m delighted with where I am from a physical point of view. It’s taken a lot of graft. It could have ended my career. I am limping at times, but you know what I’m like. It’s not for a lack of trying. I’m very proud of walking out in an England shirt.
People will comment [about his place in the team] but I’ll do what I’ll do.
It’s been a good day, the weather may or may not come but we’ve done everything we can. The approach has been questioned at times but we’ve stuck to our guns all the way through.
People will have comments on the way I bat – they always have. That’ll carry on. Yeah, you can leave them to their comments and I’ll keep doing what I do out in the middle.
England are in a commanding position after another terrific day but their prospects of squaring the series, even from this supreme position, is dependent as much on the Manchester weather for the final two days as it is on their unquenchable aggression. Jonny Bairstow’s blitz enabled them to build a lead of 275 as they passed 500 in a home Ashes Test for the first time since 1985 and then Mark Wood’s three for 17 to leave Australia without Khawaja, Warner, Smith and Wood and 162 runs behind was another stellar contribution from England’s series game-changer.
But tomorrow looks like a washout. If they can get out there for four hours in Sunday, they can still win this. Australia, meanwhile, will be praying for rain.
Moeen will bowl the final over and drops too short. Labuschagne slaps it for a single. Marsh, the Bison, plays out the rest of the over defensively. Some nice drift and dip for Moeen, searching for some rough made by Starc’s boots.
Australia trail by 162 runs.
Labuschagne slaps the first ball away for a single behind square, earning Anderson the opportunity of trying to diddle Marsh with reverse. Australia’s all-rounder defends it well with an angled bat and a good stride.
Labuschagne pulls Wood for a single and the bowler asks his captain whether he wants him to continue round the wicket and banging the ball into Marsh. Stokes confirms the plan and Wood bounds in with bouncers. Marsh easily evades two then plays the third down solidly off his chest, which prompts Stokes to bring himself up to leg gully and stick Brook at bat-pad. Wood concludes with a yorker that Marsh digs out.
Play continues until 6.43pm which should give us one more over from Wood if he can manage it. He looks cooked.
Anderson replaces Woakes for the penultimate over.
Just the no-ball off the first six but the Janus-faced nature of the pitch is playing into England’s hands. Some balls are sticking, a few are taking off, the former bringing drag-ons into play. Marsh does clip one off the edge into his front pad but the leg-guard absorbs the risk.
England lead by 165.
As Ricky Ponting points out, had he kept his eyes open, Head would have seen that ball did not leap up as high as he thought it might, so dropping his hands actually counted against him. The ball was 91mph. Enter Mitchell Marsh and Wood immediately switches to a different approach, looking for reverse, pitching it up. Marsh defends a couple, leaves one and then flicks a single off his laces to get off the mark.
Head c Duckett b Wood 1  Brilliant from Wood, a bouncer from round the wicket, angling towards Head’s Adam’s apple. We know from when he got hit in the first innings that he takes his eyes off the ball and he does so here, flapping his hands up to protect him and splicing it to the expertly placed Duckett at gully.  FOW 108/4
Thanks to Greg Wilcox for covering that last over. England continue to remove the slips for Head and post men out on the pull. Woakes duly delivers on his ribs with Bairstow standing legside but Head gets bat on it and works it fine for a single. Up come two slips for Labuschagne who defends the fuller ones then swivels to pull a shorter ball in front of square for four.
It’s Wood to continue, as you’d expect after his last over, the first two deliveries are back-of-a-length balls that Labuschagne gets in behind well. The third is too straight and the Australian Smith impressionist times it beautifully, the ball racing to the mid-wicket boundary for four. That brings up the ton for the tourists, though this is all about batting out time for them and hoping Mother Nature helps out. Wood manages a wide that brings out a smile in Bairstow (it was wider than a cocky Essex teenager...) before the over is out.
Woakes clonks Labuschagne on the helmet with a surprise bouncer. He says he hit it but if he did it was the faintest of top edges. On comes the physio. He’s all right.
For all his rockets, Wood removed Smith with a cross-seam bouncer that didn’t come through as quickly as the great batsman expected. Because there were two men out on the hook, Smith wantd to play it fine with a controlled pat rather than swinging through 90 degress with full-blooded force. Wood ratchets up the pace and has Head hopping across the crease. Double change: Woakes replaces Moeen.
That comment in over 22 about saving Wood for later making no sense? What do I know? Stokes knows.
Smith c Bairstow b Wood 17  It wasn’t reverse at all but a legside strangle. He went to pull one angled across him, scratched a top-edge and walked before the umpire raised his finger.  FOW 97/3
Mo tempts Smith into the injudicious mow/drag across the line that had him caught at short midwicket in Leeds but this time the ball falls well short of the fielder. Wood is switching ends to replace Anderson.
Labuschagne plays a Root-esque dabby glide through gully for four but before that final ball, Anderson had been exemplary, testing him with wobble and reverse outside off, creating doubt. Had he played that scoring shot at one that swung late as some did, there might have been an edge.
No turn for Moeen apart from one ball to Warner in this innings. Dropping short, he needs Wood to save boundaries galloping to his right at cover sweeper as they milk him for three singles and a pair of deuces.
Australia trail by 185.
Stokes posts himself at short mid off for Labuschagne as Anderson continues to strive for reverse. Anderson beats him when he plays and misses at a fuller one. Anderson hasn’t taken wickets here but he has bowled very well. Labuschagne whisks a straight one that doesn’t swing through midwicket for three and Smith ends the over with an extravagant, Jedi leave. Moeen Ali will replace Wood ... already.
Heeeeeere’s Jonny!
Goodness me. Wood arrows one into off-stump from wide on the crease, Labuschagne leaves on length which ultimately proves a shrewd move but mercy! It was close. It missed the off bail by a gnat’s. Wood throws his hands up to his head and bends his knees as he summons Edvard Munch levels of distress. Poor lad.
Time for drinks.
And DK was right. Anderson hoops one away from Labuschagne as he completes his fourth maiden in eight overs. Much fuller now, using the breeze to help it veer into the right-handers then shaping it away.
Wood starts in the late 80s, angling it across Labuschagne who has a flick but doesn’t connect. He pats the next one off his hip for a single and puts Smith on strike. Wood squares him up but he still gets a single to cover. Labuschagne flicks for a single. Dinesh Karthik spots reverse swing and suggests that was what Stokes was waiting for.
Mark Wood has finally returned for his second over, the 26th of Australia’s innings, and from a different end. The reasoning must be that he is going to reverse swing into the right-hander, and try to pin Steve Smith lbw, helped by the wind for a reverse inswinger.

Maiden for Anderson. Right. Good. Here comes Wood.
That’s the end of the dot ball medley. Smith drives two through mid-off, Stokes saving the boundary with a smart stop, and then whisks four through midwicket with impeccable timing. Woakes pitches it up, still tailing it in to the right-handers. Tight bowling after the earlier aberration when he strayed on to middle.
Not only would Wood rattle Australia, he would also stir the crowd up. Seems strange he hasn’t been used again. Is it because Smith and Labuschagne  are more at risk when they’re complacent?
Labuschagne is batting out of his crease to Anderson who is shaping the ball into the right-hander. The right-hander is playing it fairly comfortably but without piercing the infield. Another maiden. Woakes will continue to Smith.
Unexpected bounce for Woakes to Smith and the ball jumps up and hits the bat handle just above the splice, making him pull his bottom hand away as if stung. It’s a maiden for Woakes, his third.
Anderson is coming on for Broad, not Wood. This makes no sense.
Steve Smith is skittish again at the start of his innings which would suggest Mark Wood for a burst might be the best option. But Broad continues for now. Smith moves back and across and slaps three through cover then Labuschagne tucks into a Broad 78mph long hop, gobbling up the pie on the pull for four.
Woakes elicits a genuine edge from Smith who is saved by Root and the third umpire’s uncertainty. Shame for Woakes who is bowling beautifully.
The old foreshortening will always favour the batsman but Root wasn’t sure either.
Smith c Root b Woakes 0  Root is unsure. I think he probably caught it but it won’t be given as the camera seems to hint that it was grounded. Fair enough. It was a very tight call.
Lovely shot from Labuschagne to nail Broad down the ground with a fetching on-drive. He tucks two off his pads and then defends into the ground. As the ball bounced back off the pitch it looped back towards his stumps and he tapped it away rather than let it threaten the stumps.
First runs off Woakes when he drops short and Warner pans him through midwicket for four so Woakes returns to that nagging line, seam proud and playing with Warner’s ability to be decisive about the location of his off stump. Superb bowling and Warner departs, having made another decent start, for an inconsequential score.
Warner b Woakes 28  Drags it on. Beaten outside off by the preceding delivery which was the perfect line across the left hander and he flinched his hands towards it, Woakes goes an inch straighter and fuller, leaving Warner in no man’s land over whether to play or not. He pushes tentatively at it and plays on. FOW 54/2
Now there’s the uneven bounce. Labuschagne is left groping after a daisycutter, a worm-burner, from Broad shoots through but, unlike  Root’s, whistles past off stump. They run a bye. After Warner works one off his hip, Labuschagne again faces a grubber. Didn’t keep as low as the first but he had to adjust in a bit of a flap and jerk his bat down quicker than he would have anticipated originally.
The crowd is having a post-Tea nap. It’s Friday which does mean a chippy tea for Mancs. Always loved that Story of Bumbles about taking Jack Simmons home from Old Trafford and dropping him at the chippy where he ordered fish, chips, fishcake and a steak pudding and asked for them open not wrapped, Bumble followed him and saw him sitting on a wall a stone’s throw from his house tucking in and said: ‘Why don’t you eat them at home?’ ‘Oh, she won’t do me any tea if I take ’em home,’ he said.
Woakes beats Warner with a jaffa, draeing him forwarsd and nibbling away to beat the edge. A second successive maiden for Woakes.
Had it been anyone else ... Australia take a quick single to mid on and Anderson, needlessly, hurls at the stumps, missing by a good three yards and the ball rattles away for four overthrows. Broad is steaming but cannot give Anderson a blast, which makes it funnier still. He would have blow-torched anyone else ... Stokes apart. A rare ‘5’ in the book for Warner.
‘He bowls a heavy ball,’ they used to say about Gus Fraser. Anyone who has batted knows what it means. Not high pace but consistently jars the wrists and forearms. Woakes does the same with good nip and bounce. Nasser thinks Woakes is on here because it was from this end that Hazlewood extracted the uneven bounce. Nothing untoward yet as Marnus defends on his toes.
Well, well, well. Wood is replaced after one over by Stuart Broad. Doesn’t seem to have much logic other than David Warner being on strike. Duckett is back on the field, Warner, whose technique was the subject of the tea analysis after Ricky Ponting observed that his stance has grown so wide over the past few years that he is unbalanced, defends comfortably, those kind of positive defensives, tapped to fielders. Broad has a leg slip in for the one angled across Warner but doesn’t use that line this over, which ends in a maiden.
Chris Woakes gets the nod at the Brian Statham End, having done his best work on Wednesday at t’other end.
Another memorable session in this glorious Ashes series. High octane batting from Jonny Bairstow and raw pace from Mark Wood left England in a perfect position to level the series from here.
Not many batsmen have made an unbeaten 99 and walked off the field smiling as widely as Bairstow who laid some demons to rest by bludgeoning four sixes and ten fours to send the crowd wild and rub Australian noses in the Old Trafford dirt.
Bairstow was 49 when last man James Anderson came in, and belted his next ball for a flat six off Mitchell Starc. The field scattered, every man was on the rope as Pat Cummins chased his tail. Bairstow made light work of the biggest boundaries in the country by slapping the ball into the stands as suddenly a century became a possibility as Ben Stokes prepared to declare.
On 98 Bairstow hit to long off and pedalled fast for a two but it was not quite there and was left helpless as Anderson was leg before to Cameron Green.
Cummins recorded his worst figures, and Australia were pasted at 5.4 an over, losing it completely in a last wicket stand of 66 in 8.1 overs, conceding too many easy byes as Bairstow farmed the strike and the fielding side lost control. Only once before have Australia conceded a worse economy rate in Test cricket.
Did England bat on too long given the weather forecast? Only time will tell but they are in such a strong position because they have played brilliant cricket, and with a long evening session ahead they can take big strides towards victory.
Mark Wood does it again. That extra pace is having an impact. It’s exciting to watch. Not so much fun to face. England have dominated these last two days. So much has been said about the forecast. England were like a hurricane with the bat. Wood is like lightning with the ball. Australia are in the fight of their careers right now.
England all over Australia for another session. A superb onslaught from Jonny Bairstow was followed by a breakthrough by their 90mph+ man and signs that once the effects of the roller have worn off he, Woakes and Moeen may make hay this evening. England, let us not forget, also have crickets’ most successful player on their side in this Test: S.Coreboard-Pressure.
Play resumes at 4.15.
Two good stops at short cover by Brook save runs but Warner smacks away the low full toss for three through midwicket. Brook goes to short leg for the right-handed Labuschagne and fires in his arm ball that skids through. It hurries Labuschagne but he manages to get back and jam his bat down in time.
Time for tea. Australia trail by 236.
Pace scrambles minds and the extra bounce does for Khawaja too. Enter Labsuchagne who is treated and greeted by two bouncers which he evades but when Wood pitches up, Labuschagne is squared up by one that shot through low and it flies off a leading edge down to third man for four.
Khawaja c Bairstow b Wood 18  Just a feather as he fenced at it. Khawaja didn’t think he hit it and reviewed but he did, no’ but just.  FOW 32/1
Khawaja c Barstow b Wood
Warner clubs Moeen down the ground for four but Moeen follows it up with a beauty that was slower, drifted in, dipped and ripped, beating Warner;s forward defensive and hitting him on the pad – sadly, too high for England to turn their shouts into an appeal. Duckett was hurt fielding that edge in the previous over. It clouted him on the knee and he has to go off for a rub.
The last ball of the over is a low full toss and Warner skelps it fo four.
James Anderson continues round the wicket and is, as Michael Atherton points out with a super slow motion clip, holding it loosely to try to rotate the ball backwards after eh snaps his wrist at the release to enhance the chances of it swinging. No big movement yet but he does find Khawaja’s edge but he plays it with such a soft grip that it lands 3ft short of Duckett at third slip.
Khawaja, very deep in his crease, uses the angle of one England’s off-spinner fires on to middle to flick it off his pads fine for four. He can’t find his length in the over, trying several of then as he’s patted and cuffed for four singles as well as the boundary.
Bairstow, rather than cursing the man who left him high and dry on 99, is giving the bowler heaps of boosting. ‘Come on Jimmy Anderson,’ he says using the full name usually reserved for parents’ use during a proper telling off. He then uses Anderson’s mother and father’s preferred designation and adds a unique geographic locator: ‘Come on James Anderson from the James Anderson End.’
It’s a decent over from JM Anderson, a maiden and giving Khawaja the hurry-up with a yorker when he comes round the wicket and ramming one on to his hip bone from over.
Ben Stokes calls up Moeen Ali as first change.
Encouragement for Broad when Warner goes feeling for one but spends the majority of the maiden targeting leg stump or a leg-side strangle.
Warner pops a single off his thighpad as Anderson perseveres, mainly with the fuller length of the past 15 months but is shaping largely to leg from over the wicket to the left-handers.
Broad isn’t bowling as quick as Anderson but has more nip and carry because of his action and height. He tries a yorker at Warner but it isn’t perfectly precise and Warner flicks it off his toes for a single.
I think an early change may reap dividends here. Anderson ought to be better with an older ball. Wood’s pace with a very hard ball would be more unsettling but they might be waiting for the effects of the heavy roller to wear off.
Anderson sticks out the right boot to stop a Khawaja defensive, knocks it up and plays keepie-uppie for 10 seconds, five volleys before pouching it.
The ball ought to swing more after 10 overs once the lacquer is off. Broad chases down a lovely Kahawaj on drive and flicks it back with the ring and little fingers of his left hand before crashing knee-first into the rope. They run three.
Good response from Australia so far. They look confident, the opposite of how they were 25 minutes ago.
Hard to know where to start for Australia. England’s run rate was the second most expensive Australia have ever conceded in a Test innings, after Brendon McCullum’s extraordinary hundred in his final Test innings in 2016. Pat Cummins has never been hit for so many runs. It’s really hard to think of anything he did right there.

Khawaja pushes a single to mid-on and the crowd roars in anticipation of Broad v Warner. He’s got a breeze blowing from left to right, his bandana is flapping in it. Good nut first up to Warner, sipping through with good carry. Warner walks across to the next one to whip it to mid-on for a single.
Broad is looking to trap Khawaja on the crease with a fuller length but, unusually for Khawaja, he walks down and square drives it handsomely for four. Shot!
The first ball jumped up a bit higher than Khawaja expected but he jabs it down off his waist, then works a single off his toes. Warner, batting out of his crease, defends solidly and shouts ‘No run!’ Three slips and a deep gully. Anderson pitches the last one up and Warner again defends. Tea will be at 3.55 because of the earlier rain.
Stuart Broad will share the new ball. Of course he will.
Jonny Bairstow was hugged as he left the field and again when he bounded out in his keeping gear. The heavy roller has one last lap. James Anderson will open the bowling.
Ben Stokes was right again, of course. It was well worth having that last-wicket stand of 66 off 8.1 overs because it boosted Jonny Bairstow’s morale and deflated Australia’s even more.
It was a purple passage of play, especially when Steve Smith was standing in front of the temporary stand, its spectators were singing “We saw you cry on the telly!”, then Bairstow hooked a six into the base of the stand. Smith and Marnus Labuschagne had to leave the field and burrow under the covers to get the ball back, village-style.
The wheels flew off Australia’s machine. Alex Carey was found wanting when Baristow, three times, scurried through for a bye to get James Anderson off strike and Carey did not take his glove off to throw. Only a single for Bairstow was missing, but then nothing in cricket is perfect.
The only two England batsmen to make 99 not out against Australia are Boycott and Bairstow. I believe Sir Geoffrey’s was in the reunification three-match series of 1979-80 and hence not in the Ashes. Bob Willis told him he would take Geoff Dymock if Boycott kept out DK Lillee. So Geoffrey did, only to watch aghast as Willis promptly got out to the left-arm medium pacer.
Ha! England steal another bye off the first ball as Anderson lets it through to Carey and his underarm misses. ‘Take one glove off,’ says Ricky Ponting for the third time. Too true.
Bairstow drives, wants two but it isn’t there. Anderson is stranded when sent back but mid-off throws the ball to the wrong end. Anderson on strike, Bairstow on 99.
Anderson is pinned and Bairstow jogs off 99*
England lead by 275.
The game’s afoot!
Anderson lbw b Green 5
Anderson lbw b Green Bairstow stranded on 99? Looks plumb
Cummins sprays another down the legside with Anderson facing and again Carey can do nothing about it as it flies down for four more byes. They steal another bye off the next ball as it goes through to the keeper and Carey can’t throw the stumps down when Bairstow’s looking at him. Easier when his back was turned, eh Alex?
Bairstow cuts the next ball and chips it off the bottom edge for four through third man.
Here come a few spots of rain.
One ball to come. In comes the field to deny him a single so Bairstow climbs into cut, slamming it for a one-bounce four to move to 98 ... but not on strike.
Here’s Cameron Green. He bounces Anderson who drops his hands to deflect it between slip and silly point and they steal a single as the ball carroms away. Smith cannot believe it.
Bairstow turns down three singles as Green changes it up with bouncers, wide-ish ones, yorkers, pace on, pace off. The last ball is short and Bairstow pulls it fine for four but is off strike. The partnership is 51 off 39.
England have been here before: at Perth and Sydney especially, when it has felt like Australia are batting on merely for the purpose of humiliating their opponents. But now, the agony is all Australia’s, encapsulated by the sight of James Anderson waltzing down the wicket and pulling Pat Cummins disdainful through midwicket. This might just be the moment that the Old Trafford crowd have enjoyed more than any other this Test.

Bairstow leaves singles un-run off the first two deliveries. Dot balls in name but not in nature. And then pulls the third for six with a short-arm jab. The power of the man. What a Test this has been for the three most maligned cricketers in this team: Moeen, YJB and Zak C, the ones some commenters wanted to be dropped.
Then Bairstow plays the most remarkable stroke, pure T20, almost a golf stroke, launching a mowed drive over midwicket for six!
Stokes behind the glass on the dressing room says ‘That’s massive!’ It was! Almost out of the ground.
Cummins tries to stay out of his arc and sprays four byes down the legside to end the over.
Whatever happens from here in this game, it is fantastic news for England that Jonny Bairstow is back in this series. He was starting to become a joke figure after all the nonsense at Lord’s and a quiet game at Headingley. Bodes well for the Oval. There won’t be any talk about dropping him after this game.
Hazlewood has nine men on the boundary plus himself and the wicketkeper. After two dot balls, Jonny turning down singles, Bairstow hooks him for six!
Smith and Labuschagne have to climb over the hoardings to retrieve the ball and they’re roasted by the crowd with the greatest hits, ‘Cry on the telly’ etc.
Hazlewood tries a slow bouncer and Barstow pulls for two then pushes a drive to long off for a single. In come half a dozen fielders for Anderson as he faces the final ball, which he pokes down through gully.
England lead by 239.
Cummins follows Anderson with a bouncer. Anderson walks down and pulls it for four! The next bouncer vaults over Anderson’s shoulder and the No11 ducks the next.
Anderson defends the next two off his midriff well. One to go and again it’s a short one as Australia go one-dimensional. Anderson sways inside the line.
The England balcony looks ready to start fielding imminently.
Hazlewood bounces Anderson from round the wicket and he fends it off his face. Hazlewood tries another bouncer and Bairstow calls him through for a bye when it sailed over Jimmy’s head. Australia are not happy about that, not happy with themselves.
Bairstow late cuts the next ball for four, using the pace. Starc dived to stop it but touched the rope  with his shoulder as he patted it back at full stretch.
Bairstow can’t connect when he tries to hook Hazlewood’s high bouncer. In comes the field. But, like in the preceding over, he wants to leg glance for a single but times it so well it smokes away for four.
England lead by 228. Cummins brings himself back on to try to remove Anderson.
Starc starts with a short ball and Bairstow pulls it off his midriff for six! Fifty for YJB. Starc tries the yorker and Bairstow chisels it out, shouting ‘No run!’ like Warner/Smith/Labuschagne, perhaps even parodying them.
Starc goes wider and Bairstow lets it go. Starc again forces it wide of Bairstow’s striking arc for another dot ball and then sprays one down the legside that Bairstow can’t reach with a flick.
The final ball is full and Bairstow times the pants off it, whisking it for four through midwicket. He wanted the strike but gleaned four instead.
Hazlewood is going to bounce Anderson, too, but he gets up on his toes to defend the first and sways inside the next one . He ducks the last ball of the over and I expect Bairstow will now have a slog for an over.
Broad c & b Hazlewood 7  Hazlewood sets the field for a barrage at Broad, digs one on and Broad top edges a slog sending it steepling towards short cover. Hazlewood calls for it and bags his 10th 5Wi in Tests. Here comes the Burnley Lara to a standing ovation from his own crowd. FOW 526/9
That single, which almost brought his downfall for Broad in the previous over, was his 1000th Test run against Australia. 100 Test wickets and 1,000 Test runs in Ashes matches is a hell of a feat. Only Lord Botham and Wilfred Rhodes have achieved that before for England, I think.
Broad slices two over cover and unconvincingly flat-bats a pull for a single. Bairstow pings a flick through midwicket for a single and Broad chisels one out by his feet fine for another.
England lead by 208.
Hazlewood continues his pre-lunch spell. Broad and Bairstow calmly exchange singles then Broad tees off and toes it high but safe between mid off and long on. England move 200 ahead. Bairstow takes a stride towards Hazlewood and carves two through cover which would have been four but for Green’s agile, diving stop.
Three balls to go. The first of which hoops into Bairstow’s pads and goes down for four leg byes. Bairstow drills a drive for a single and Broad gets up to fence a short ball into the offside for another.
And play will resume in a couple of minutes.
Declare now! Old Trafford is not a conventional swinging ground but a strong crosswind, suitable for an outswing bowler from the James Anderson End, like James Anderson. Good “overheads”, an England lead of 191, time to make the most of the last two sessions by bowling.

And the umpires are coming out for an inspection. The hover still refused to hover. Poor Sir Christopher Cockerell. What have they done to his baby?
The hover cover has broken down!
They are having to resort to tarpaulins.
Wait on! They’re jump-starting it now.
This should be the last shower of the day according to the satellite.

Starc has the newish ball, hangs it outside Bairstow’s off stump and he taps a drive out to the cover sweeper for a single. Broad takes a leg-bye off an inswinger and, after Bairstow defends then ensures the ball doesn’t roll back on to his stumps, the rain thickens and much to Broad’s disgust, the umpires take them off.
Rain stopped play.

Bagchi in for Smyth. The players are out. England bat on, Jonny Bairstow on strike.
By Nick Hoult at Old Trafford
Will England declare at lunch? They should. It is time start the job of chipping out the Australian wickets and levelling the series because the weather for the next two days is either wet, very wet or extremely wet depending on which forecast you believe.
England have 500 on the board for the first time in a home Ashes Test since 1985. They added 122 this morning and this is their fastest 500 at home against any opposition since the 1985 Ashes. Australia were on the backfoot throughout that session, opting for damage limitation mode after such a beating on day two. They delayed the second new ball, spread the field and tried to hold on to the coattails of the Bazballers.
It worked to a certain extent but it is quite something to see the world champions and the sport’s alpha males reduced to hanging in and hoping for the best. Stokes made fifty, Harry Brook too and Jonny Bairstow was just finding his range at lunch.
There is plenty of swing and the cracked pitch is offering variable bounce. The bowling conditions are perfect. Time for James Anderson to turn up.
Just a slight squally shower blowing through at lunch, so the hover cover is coming on. No word yet on a declaration, but this might just clarify things. The wicket will have got a bit of moisture on it there before the cover made it on.
After another eventful morning, England lead by 189 runs. Australia bowled well for the most part, Hazlewood and Cummins in particular, and England had to manufacture most of their boundaries with unorthodox shots.
The over rate was dreadful but there was still plenty of action: England scored 122/4 in 24 overs at a run-rate of 5.08.
Wood b Hazlewood 6 Mark Wood is bowled by the last ball before lunch. It was a good one from Hazlewood, which extracted the off stump, though he had already conceded 15 runs in the over. Bairstow hit successive boundaries with a back cut and a straight drive; England also brought up the 500 in just 95.3 overs. FOW: 506/8
This is a nice little innings for Bairstow, which has been played under relatively little pressure because of the match situation. It should make him feel a whole lot better about life going into what could be a series decider at the Oval.
Australia are bowling an orthodox line and length to Wood, who is beaten by consecutive deliveries from Starc. After running riot at Headingley, he has made 2 from 6 balls today.
Hazlewood, who dismissed Brook with the last ball of his previous over, almost takes a hat-trick when Wood is beaten by his first delivery. England lead by 171.
Woakes c Carey b Hazlewood 0 Chris Woakes goes for a golden duck. He pushed defensively at a lovely outswinger from Hazlewood, the sort he’ll hope to bowl this afternoon, and edged through to Alex Carey. England won’t mind this at all. FOW: 486/7
Bairstow inside edges a Starc inswinger past leg stump for four. This is his second highest score of the series: 78, 20, 16, 10, 12, 5 and now 23*.
Another classic inswinger beats Bairstow, who then times a superb boundary through midwicket. A Bairstow assault is imminent.
So, Brook goes for a useful 100-ball 61, and Chris Woakes is the new batsman.
Brook c Starc b Hazlewood 61 Harry Brook tries to force the pace and loses his wicket. He flapped a hook to long leg, where Starc took a superbly judged catch just inside the boundary. The crowd jeered when they saw the replay, though I’ve no idea why - his back foot was nowhere near the sponge. That was all a bit weird. FOW: 474/6
Australia take the second new ball, which should enliven this slightly sleepy morning. There’s immediate swing for Mitchell Starc, a mixed blessing for Australia given the match situation.  Bairstow, who has been dismissed 11 times by Starc in Tests, defends respectfully.
That light shower has passed through Old Trafford. The offspinner Travis Head is coming on, which should mean sixes, wickets or both. For now Brook and Bairstow are happy with two singles apiece.
Since you asked, the last time England scored 500 against Australia was during the run-orgy of 2010-11, when they did it four times. But they haven’t done it in a home Ashes Test since 1985.
Bairstow is starting to loosen his shoulders. He swivel-pulls Hazlewood smoothly for two, then cracks a cut to the deep point to move to 13 from 16 balls. Brook has 56 from 90 and, most important of all, England lead by 150.
Mitchell Starc replaces Cummins, who bowled a good spell of 4-0-12-1. Five low-risk runs from the over. It feels like everyone is waiting for Jonny Bairstow to tee off.
It has just started raining at Old Trafford, though it’s very light and play will continue for now.
Hazlewood replaces Green. After mistiming a couple of attacking strokes, Brook walks across to hook a boundary to fine leg. England haven’t been fluent this morning, yet they have still scored 73 runs in 15 overs. Imagine writing that sentence in 1991; you’d have been laughed out of the Long Room.
How good has the contest been between the two captains?  Brilliant to watch. Two great players going head to head. One of the great contests of this series so far. This is fantastic Test cricket to watch. Seeing how the players perform under Ashes pressure is what Test cricket is all about.
Cummins has bowled well this morning, as Tim said below, although a single from Bairstow brings up his century off only 19.2 overs.
A more significant milestone is Harry Brook’s fifty, which he reaches with a quick single: 80 balls, 4x4.
Six from the over, none in boundaries. Cummins’ economy rate in this series is 4.02, easily the worst of his career. He has never previously gone at three an over in an Ashes series, never mind four.
Pat Cummins has bowled better so far today, and is getting some nip with the old ball, and was rewarded with the wicket of his counterpart Ben Stokes. But Australia won’t be enjoying signs that the pitch is becoming harder to bat on. You’d think England will declare at lunch - which would save the two overs lost for a change of innings - at the latest. The lead is already 130. Australia haven’t yet taken the second new ball - expect them to do so soon, though there’s always a risk that it could be more expensive as the ball pings off the bat.
Brook, on the run, swipes Green over mid-on for four. His fledgling average when batting at No5 in Tests is 78.23. Of those who have played at least 10 innings in that position, only Rishabh Pant (80.11) averages more.
Green hits Bairstow in the stomach with a sharp nipbacker. There’s a little bit in this pitch, and it’ll be interesting to see what happens if/when Australia take the new ball.
With England leading by 130, it’s time for drinks.
Bairstow likes to take 10-20 balls to get his eye in before teeing off. He gets off the mark with a simple clip to leg.
Australia are having a decent little spell: 17/1 off the last six overs. The decision to stick with the old ball is working.
Stokes b Cummins 51 England lose their first wicket of the day. Stokes heaves across the line at Cummins, misses and is bowled. There’s no celebration from Cummins, but Stokes swishes his bat as he walks off. England lead by 120, and heeeeeeeeeeeeere’s Jonny. FOW: 437/5
Brook, walking down the track to Green, is almost bowled behind his legs. Aside from those three boundaries in four balls off Starc, he has struggled to time this old ball. He has 40 from 71 balls, Stokes 51 from 73.
Stokes pushes Cummins for a single to reach a comfortable half-century from 72 balls. That’s all I’ve got.
Bumped into Glenn McGrath in the lift just before play. He said that he’d have liked to see Australia adopt more variations - one-day skills, essentially, like slower balls and yorkers, which Mitchell Starc is particularly adept at - yesterday. He also highlighted, as other have, Pat Cummins’ tendency to follow the ball and Australia’s apparent inability to stick to a ball for more than a couple of overs. Bowling conditions look much better today, which will please England more than Australia.
Green continues with the soft old ball. He continues to ram the ball halfway down, and England continue to take easy singles. After five runs off the first deliveries, Stokes is beaten by a delivery that bursts from a length. He shouts “Woah!” and snaps his head back, a slightly exaggerated gesture for the benefit of the Australian batsmen.
Pat Cummins assumes the position in place of Mitchell Starc, with no slips in place and men spread all round the boundary.
Stokes charges the first ball and misses a lusty yahoo, and Cummins concedes just a couple from an accurate first over. The new ball is due. Not sure Australia want it though.
It is staggering. Such fields might be seen at the end of a long innings, but not BEFORE the second new ball is due.
Cam Green replaces Hazlewood, with instructions to bowl short and shorter. Brook and Stokes help themselves to five low-risk runs. Five an over, against Australia, sans risk. I have no idea what has happened to English cricket.
Brook gets his first boundary of the innings from the 52nd delivery, driving Starc imperiously through the covers.
The second comes off the next ball, a low full toss from round the wicket that is put away between extra cover and mid-off, and he makes it 12 from the over with a deft steer to third man. Lovely shot.
Stokes gets four more with a smear through midwicket off Hazlewood. He has played some some extremely agricultural strokes this morning, and that’s just fine. It’s not how, it’s how many, and how quickly.
This old ball is hard to hit, hence Stokes playing such unorthodox shots, so Australia may well stick with it. England have scored 26 from five overs this morning, and it feels like they’re going slowly.
Another run-out chance goes begging for Australia. Brook, sent back by Stokes, was miles short of his ground when Cummins’ throw from mid-on whistled past the stumps.
Brook has been quiet this morning. I suspect he’s waiting for the second new ball, due in four overs, before proceeding straight to fifth gear. That’s if Australia take it; I’m not sure I would.
Stokes charges Hazlewood and pulls furiously to the midwicket boundary. That brings up the England 400 and also the fifty partnership.
The third umpire Kumar Dharmasena has confirmed that Stokes wouldn’t have been out even if Australia had appealed for that run-out chance, because Carey’s gloves dislodged the bails.
Interesting moment, there, with that run out chance. Would Australia have appealed if they hadn’t had their spirit questioned at Lord’s? The ball did hit the stumps, although it was surely Carey’s gloves that dislodged it. Either way, a missed chance of England’s most dangerous batsman.
Mitchell Starc, who went off with a shoulder injury last night, is fit to bowl. Stokes charges his second ball and slugs it through midwicket for four. “Absolute filth from the England captain,” deadpans Mark Butcher on Sky Sports.
Starc’s response is a thrilling yorker which Stokes inside-edges on the boot. And then Stokes survives a run-out chance! He tried to steal a second run to deep cover and would have been out had Carey not fumbled Neser’s throw. That’s a rare error from him.
The ball actually hit the stumps at the same time as Carey’s gloves, with Stokes still short of his ground. But it looked like it was the gloves that dislodged the bails. I’ve never seen that before. Australia didn’t appeal so it wasn’t sent upstairs to the third umpire.

Welcome to our live coverage for the Friday of the British Grand Prix, which will take in two practice sessions in Friday. First practice starts at 11.30am BST and second practice is at 4pm, with both sessions running for an hour. The last couple of editions of the British Grand Prix have been superb races for different reasons, with Hamilton and Verstappen’s clash in 2021 (with Hamilton winning) and then a thrilling race in which Carlos Sainz won his maiden grand prix for Ferrari, not forgetting the drama which took us to that point.
Is that going to be the same this year? Well, it would surely take something unusual to happen to Max Verstappen for that to be the case. However, if that did happen then it would likely be a fascinating race. Red Bull have won each and every of the nine races this year, with Verstappen winning seven of those, including the last five in a row. Sergio Perez’s title challenge has melted after a decent start and, given their respective driving styles, we shouldn’t expect the Dutchman to have too much competition from his team-mate this weekend.
Who might provide Verstappen with something to think about? Well, it’s a tight battle between Aston Martin, Mercedes and Ferrari behind Red Bull, but last week’s Austrian Grand Prix showed that the Red Bull is still an absolute mile ahead of anyone else. Ferrari had a more encouraging weekend at the Red Bull Ring, to go with some decent race pace at the previous race in Canada, but Charles Leclerc was not really in Verstappen’s league. Verstappen had enough of a gap towards the end of the race to pit for fresh tyres and do the fastest lap.
Mercedes had another difficult weekend, although that is perhaps down to some set-up strangeness and unusual conditions that made the car look worse than it actually was. The W14 should suit this track a little better, but it is hard to expect that they will be fighting for victory after being nearly 50 seconds down on Verstappen at the chequered flag. Indeed, before Verstappen pitted, Russell was about to be lapped by the Red Bull driver.
First practice gets under way in a little under an hour, so we will be here for all the build-up, live updates and reaction from that session and second practice later in the day.

Dame Alison Rose had a spring in her step as she greeted NatWest staff and shareholders in April.
Speaking at an annual gathering at the bank’s sprawling headquarters on the outskirts of Edinburgh, the chief executive had recently received one of the highest awards in the King’s first honours list.
She was also the first NatWest boss to get an annual bonus since the financial crisis.
Since winning the top job in 2019, Dame Alison had been feted not just for her banking nous but for championing corporate “values” and “purpose”, buzzwords embraced heartily by fellow blue chip executives.
“Our values are at the heart of how we deliver our purpose-led strategy,” she told the gathering.
Under her leadership, NatWest had come to describe itself as “a relationship bank for a digital world”. Its values are “being inclusive, curious, robust, sustainable and ambitious”.
They are laudable aims. Yet these same values would be Dame Alison’s undoing, as they were applied in ways she may never have imagined.
In a now widely reported dossier first revealed by The Telegraph, overzealous employees at Coutts, a private bank and subsidiary of NatWest, explained at length why they believed the group’s inclusion or “ESG” (environmental, social and governance) policies meant they should no longer provide services to Nigel Farage.
His offence? The pugnacious former Brexit Party leader had made a string of public remarks that did not “align to the bank’s purpose and values”.
They included comments in support of Donald Trump, his sharing of a “transphobic” sketch by comedian Ricky Gervais on Twitter, and what Coutts concluded were his “xenophobic, chauvinistic and racist views”.
The ensuing scandal as Farage went public with his “debanking” has morphed into a media firestorm that NatWest has struggled to contain.
Dame Alison was forced to resign after she admitted to leaking details of Farage’s banking situation to a BBC journalist.
It is a fiasco that has thrust corporate values and so-called “woke capitalism” into the spotlight, underlining the risks companies can expose themselves to when they wade into politics and social causes.
NatWest is by no means alone.
The mantra of “purpose” and ESG (environmental, social and governance) has been enthusiastically embraced by the jet-setting class in recent years, with advocates claiming it helps to boost customer trust and motivate staff.
In 2021, Alan Jope stood up and declared that Hellmann’s mayonnaise, a best selling product ever since its invention in a New York deli 108 years earlier, had finally found its purpose.
It was not simply to be a condiment that people used in sandwiches, salads and other meals, the then-chief executive of Unilever insisted.
“Fighting against food waste – that is the purpose of Hellmann’s,” Jope said, as the company unveiled a campaign highlighting how the product could be combined with leftovers in the fridge.
“Hellmann’s believes food is too good to be wasted and food waste should be socially unacceptable,” the company’s website said. “We want to help people to make any food delicious, so they don’t have to waste any.”
There was just one problem. While Jope and Unilever were busy dreaming up purposes for Domestos disinfectant (“to win the war against unsafe sanitation”) and Knorr stock cubes (“reinventing food for humanity”), investors were growing frustrated with the share price – which was going nowhere.
It prompted scathing criticism from Terry Smith, the star fund manager, who claimed Unilever’s “ludicrous” passion project was detracting from its day-to-day performance.
“A company that feels it has to define the purpose of Hellmann’s mayonnaise has clearly lost the plot,” the entrepreneur wrote.
“The Hellmann’s brand has existed since 1913 so we would guess that by now consumers have figured out its purpose (spoiler alert – salads and sandwiches).”
The row is one of many examples of companies getting more deeply involved in social causes, not always with success.Food and drink giant Mars was ridiculed for “going woke” last year when it redesigned the iconic M&M characters.
Gone were the green M&M’s knee-high boots, which had been replaced by a pair of trainers. The heel on the brown M&M’s stilettos were also cut to a short stub, reflecting what Mars claimed was “a more dynamic, progressive world”.
The company later backtracked following a high-profile backlash, giving its so-called “spokescandies” another redesign.
In some cases, companies have been criticised for what critics say are performative gestures, leading to allegations of “greenwashing” and “rainbow-washing” – where corporations back gay rights or environmental causes in western countries but take little real action or remain silent on them in other markets.
It is prompting businesses and their shareholders to question the wisdom of politicising everything, while Conservative politicians eye an opportunity to attack left-wing groupthink in boardrooms.
Luke Tryl, UK director of More In Common, a charity that tracks debates about contentious issues in Britain. says: “People welcome meaningful examples of corporate social responsibility, but what they don’t want is virtue signalling.
“But there’s a real grey area in which kind of inclusion initiatives fall into taking a political stance and which fall into actually just being a good corporate citizen – and that is a really tricky line for businesses to walk.”
Despite the jargon, the principles underpinning ESG are hardly new.
From the Cadbury family’s decision to build homes, parks and libraries for chocolate factory workers to Lord Leverhulme’s model village for his employees at Port Sunlight, Merseyside, there’s a long tradition of businesses supporting their staff and championing social causes.
But the birth of the modern ESG movement has been credited to a paper published by the United Nations in 2004. “Who Cares, Wins” claimed that companies applying these principles were not just doing the right thing but also made themselves more competitive.
The ideas have gained traction in the C-suite ever since, as big businesses seek to downplay the “greed is good” culture that critics blamed for the financial crisis.
Perhaps no British bank embodied this transformation as much as NatWest, previously known as Royal Bank of Scotland.
Under former chief executive Fred “the Shred” Goodwin – dubbed “Britain’s most notorious banker” – RBS embarked on a global takeover spree, briefly making it the world’s biggest bank before it crashed spectacularly. It was bailed out in 2008 to the tune of £46bn in taxpayer cash, and Goodwin became a lightning rod for public anger.
By contrast, Dame Alison’s public image could not have been further from Goodwin’s. A bank lifer who joined as a trainee, she spent years patiently climbing the corporate ladder and, later, cleaning up the disgraced investment banking division of RBS.
When she succeeded Ross McEwan as chief executive a year later, she immediately set about replacing the RBS brand with the less toxic NatWest one, while launching a company-wide process to find the lender’s “purpose”.
“I truly believe that if you are going to lead an organisation and create an organisation that has value over the long-term, it has to be purpose-led,” she told the Blueprint for Better Business podcast last month.
“No organisation deserves to exist. We have no right to exist tomorrow unless we are creating value for all of our stakeholders, which are our customers, our communities, our colleagues, and our shareholders.”
In 2021, NatWest was one of several large British companies – alongside the National Grid, food producer Unilever, outsourcer Capita, rival lender Barclays, pensions manager Fidelity International, law firm Hogan Lovells and water supplier Severn Trent – to vow to put the needs of staff, local communities and wider society higher on agenda.
It followed a watershed moment a year earlier, when BlackRock’s chief executive, Larry Fink, announced that the fund management giant – which looks after $9 trillion in assets – now regarded sustainability as the “new standard for investing”.
Guy Jubb, an honorary professor at the University of Edinburgh, and the former head of stewardship and governance at Standard Life Investments, says well-run companies that meet ESG standards will have “the ingredients to develop longer term prosperity for their shareholders and for society”.
“If you look to companies which have had serious ESG problems, you can get an impairment in value which actually undermines wealth creation,” he adds.
There is also evidence that, on the face of it, consumers welcome efforts by companies to act more responsibly, whether that is by cutting carbon emissions or welcoming employees of all backgrounds.
“People are very supportive. The scepticism tends to come when it’s seen as being tokenistic,” says Tryl from More In Common.
But as the ESG movement has grown, and a cottage industry of consultants, spinners and auditors have sprung up around it, so too have the risks of companies getting things wrong.
Nike is arguably one of the most well-known companies in terms of its strident approach to brand activism.
The sportswear giant has created adverts criticising “the patriarchy” and showing American football star Colin Kaepernick – who famously began “taking the knee” at games to protest against racism and was sacked – with the words: “Believe in something. Even if it means sacrificing everything.”
The campaigns have won Nike plaudits from some campaigners and accusations of “woke-washing” from others, who noted that less than 10pc of the company’s own vice-presidents globally are black.
Meanwhile, ice-cream maker Ben & Jerry’s – which is owned by Unilever – faced criticism for accusing Joe Biden of “fanning the flames of war” by supporting Ukraine, and for calling on the UK Government to scrap its plans to deport illegal immigrants to Rwanda.
Sometimes, brands face criticism even for what seem like harmless gestures of support.
United Airlines last month found itself at the centre of a storm over its sponsorship of London Pride, when Just Stop Oil activists warned that they would seek to disrupt the event unless the company pulled out.
And while many British businesses have rushed to sign up to Stonewall’s Diversity Champions programme, which advises on creating inclusive workplaces, their decision to adopt the charity’s gender ideology has put them on the front line as debates rage about how society should adapt to the growing use of non-traditional pronouns and genders.
Amid a growing backlash about corporate campaigning, US Republicans have attacked companies championing ESG as “woke capitalists” and taken drastic actions, such as withdrawing state funds from money managers such as BlackRock.
Disney has found itself in a feud with Ron DeSantis, the Florida governor and potential Republican presidential nominee, after opposing laws that banned discussion of sexual orientations in schools, dubbed the “don’t say gay” bill by critics.
Companies have also left themselves open to accusations of hypocrisy, when their “purpose-led” values only seem to apply in countries where it is easy to champion them.
Some such as Unilever have been accused by the Ukrainian government of effectively helping to finance Vladimir Putin’s invasion, by refusing to quit their operations in Russia and continuing to pay taxes there.
The blowback against ESG has been so fierce in the US that Fink, BlackRock’s boss, has stopped referring to the term in his annual letters to investors. He recently complained that it has been “weaponised” by critics.
This new caution has also been reflected in mentions of ESG during earnings calls by blue chip companies, which peaked at 156 in the final quarter of 2021 but fell to 74 in the first quarter of 2023, according to data from Factset.
In the UK, meanwhile, Rishi Sunak last year vowed to tackle “woke nonsense and left-wing agitators” in public life, while ministers have mulled watering down net zero commitments in a bid to win votes.
Amid the fallout at NatWest, the Government has taken a tough line, issuing a stern readout following a meeting with banking executives – minus the recently exiled Alison Rose – warning them not to impinge on customers’ freedom of speech.
“The idea that a person could face having their account terminated for expressing their political views [is] wholly unacceptable,” the statement added.
Even within boardrooms, ESG has come under fire for the mountains of paperwork and sometimes topsy-turvy outcomes that it generates.
Elon Musk branded ESG “the devil” earlier this year when his electric car company, Tesla, scored a lower rating than a string of tobacco companies.
Oil giant Chevron achieved a higher score in the assessment, which was based on a variety of factors including green credentials, corporate governance and diversity.
Yet the stakes for companies are real, with pension funds and other top investors increasingly using ESG indexes to allocate their funds. This is despite a variety of different standards being applied by various different asset managers and audit firms.
A report published in November by Tulchan, a financial PR company, found British companies were frustrated at a “box-ticking” approach taken by investors towards ESG policies, warning it was “over-prescriptive and formulaic”.
Some felt the situation was getting so bad that they were “locked in a struggle” with investors over how to run their own businesses.
Romi Savova, chief executive and founder of financial technology provider PensionBee, supports ESG goals but thinks companies should be wary of straying too far outside their areas of focus.
“Consumers do expect businesses to be good corporate citizens and the meaning of that will be specific to each business,” she says. “But it should generally encompass issues that are material to the business, rather than any and all issues.”
For example, she says PensionBee’s customers are diverse and so the London-listed company aims to mirror that in the makeup of its own workforce.
It also campaigns on issues such as the “carer’s pension gap”, affecting people who have to take time off work to care for a loved one.
However, Sir Martin Sorrell, the advertising guru who built WPP into a global titan and now runs digital ad agency S4 Capital, warns that the current check-box nature of ESG requirements can hinder rather than help businesses.
“We’re a tiny company, we produce a 200-page annual report and a separate ESG report,” he explains. “It’s absolutely crackers.”
Different regulators all demand different standards as well. “So we have about 10 different sets of standards to comply with, and we had a board meeting yesterday where half the agenda was taken up in approving policies in relation to ESG.”
However, Sorrell says, that doesn’t mean these policies aren’t needed in some form or another – he just believes the ESG industry has gotten over-complicated.
“If you’re going to maximise long term profitability, you have to have gender equality, you have to have a fair representation of the communities in which you work, you have to take into account the interests of all stakeholders – that’s stakeholder capitalism.
“But there’s been this sort of business school over-complication of it all, when it’s really very simple. If you’re trying to build a business for the long term, you will naturally involve all stakeholders.
“So the objective is to maximise long term profitability. And that’s it. Everything else will fall into place.”
In the NatWest example, he points out, if staff were truly thinking about the long-term, they would not have chosen to debank Nigel Farage.
“It places you in an impossible position. Because, are you now going to go through every one of your customers? It’s just illogical.”
As public attitudes grow more sceptical towards “woke” corporate values, one question being debated in political circles is how much the Tories can make hay from these issues, if any.
Pollsters say the by-election in Uxbridge, where the Conservatives saw off a challenge from Labour and narrowly retained their seat, is a sign of how issues that affect voters’ wallets can be powerful swing issues.
Many residents in the borough were unhappy about the ultra-low emissions zone (Ulez) being implemented by Labour’s Sadiq Khan, the London mayor, and voted accordingly.
Some Tories believe this is a sign of more widespread opposition to net zero policies among households.
“I think the whole population recognises that we need a transition that is affordable and particularly for working families, people who are struggling to make ends meet,” says Danny Kruger, a Tory backbencher.
Yet others are concerned that this could backfire. Among those who voted Tory in 2019 and plan to vote Labour next year, more than half felt Rishi Sunak has “not gone far enough” on tackling climate change, a recent Opinium poll for The Times found.
“It would be wrong for either the Conservatives or Labour to conclude that Uxbridge was a rejection of environmental policies,” says Sir Alok Sharma, the former cabinet minister and ex-president of the Cop26 climate conference, pointing to polls like that one.
“Of course, the cost of living is front and centre right now and that is why we need to support people to make a transition.
“Ultimately the cost of ‘not zero’ will be way greater than the cost of ‘net zero’ with none of the upsides in economic growth, jobs and a cleaner environment.”
Tryl, of More In Common, says debates around topics such as gender are unlikely to make good “wedge issues” for the Tories because most voters will simply question why politicians aren’t prioritising more bread and butter issues such as the economy, the NHS and immigration.
He recalls sitting in on a focus group not long after students at an Oxford college voted to remove a portrait of Queen Elizabeth II from their common room in 2021.
Gavin Williamson, who was Education Secretary at the time, branded the move “simply absurd”.
By Tryl says politicians should avoid jumping on anti-woke bandwagons. “Someone asked, ‘Why is the Education Secretary commenting on this? Hasn’t he got better things to do?’ And everyone in the group agreed.
“The next election, given where the economy is, is going to be fought through an economic prism, and I think the danger of focusing on social issues is you start to look like you’re missing the public mood.”
A similar mood prevails towards businesses, he adds, with most consumers preferring companies to focus on providing good services and treating their own staff well.
“Before you start doing any of the other stuff and kind of pushing and trying to persuade others, actually, you should be getting your own house in order,” Tryl adds.
“There’s a big difference between demonstrating your values by, say, sponsoring something at a Pride March or getting to net zero, and using those principles to effectively drive people out – that’s where people go, ‘Business shouldn’t be doing this’.”
Before leaving NatWest, Alison Rose liked to say that “being purposeful is not about the easy decisions, it’s about the tough decisions”.
As she’d surely now testify, the consequences of those decisions can also be very tough as well.

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/golf/2023/07.title: Just Stop Oil protesters strike at the Open
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/golf/2023/07.subtitle: Golfer Billy Horschel helped to apprehend the individuals on the 17th hole at Royal Liverpool during the second round of the Championship
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/golf/2023/07.text:
Just Stop Oil protesters were wrestled away by a player before being grappled to the floor by marshals amid drama on the 17th green at the 151st Open.
American Billy Horschel, the world No 45, ignored warnings from the R&A not to get involved as he blocked a woman running on with orange powder.
The protesters – two men and one woman – tried to gain access to Hoylake’s famous par-three 17th where many believe this Open could be decided. A fourth man, a suspected accomplice, was also arrested after activists breached the lower corner of a grandstand and ran towards the green.
Spectators on the stands erected around the hole, which only measures 136 yards, booed the protesters before police eventually led the suspects away.
Witnesses, who captured some of the scenes on their mobiles, praised the no-nonsense actions of Horschel and the marshals. A plume of orange dust could be seen in the air as the protest unfolded, but stewards quickly cleared marks left on the green with a leaf blower.
Despite ignoring R&A guidance about “not doing a Bairstow”, Horschel will face no action from authorities for intervening.
One eyewitness, Claire Grimwood, from Hull, told The Telegraph that Horschel and a marshal had tackled one of the men: “The marshal ran on and got to the protester who had some orange spray, and wrestled him to the ground and then sat on him in the long grass. But the police couldn’t see them in the long grass so they had to call them over.”
She added that Horschel was cheered when he helped to remove a woman in a white top before she was handed over to police. One of the male protesters was led away in handcuffs. Another man held at the scene was ushered away without being cuffed after security officials told police to be discreet.
“I saw one run in from the bottom of the grandstands on the right of the green and two from the left and they had canisters of orange powder or something. They didn’t get right up to the flag. They were just to the edge of the green and then the marshals got hold of them and pulled them away.”
Around 20 police officers eventually descended on the scene, including some in plain-clothes.
Every eye-witness who spoke to The Telegraph had little sympathy for Just Stop Oil, which has also disrupted Wimbledon, the Ashes, rugby and snooker in recent months.  “There were a few boos from the crowd,” said Matty Campbell, 41, from Leeds. Gary Richards, 61, from the Wirral, added: “I think there’s ways and means to express themselves, but holding a tournament to ransom is not the way forward.”
The group playing the hole at the time was Horschel, Canadian Corey Conners and Swede Alex Noren. After completing his round Horschel declined to comment to the media.
A spokesperson for the R&A said: “A protester was quickly apprehended on the 17th hole and is one of four people who have been arrested by the police. Play was not disrupted and we would like to thank the marshals, players and other spectators for their vigilance and understanding as the protesters were removed.”
Players and caddies competing at the Open were via a letter from the R&A earlier this week not to take matters into their own hands should Just Stop Oil strike, with a huge security operation in action.
Significant numbers of uniformed and plain-clothes police are patrolling the championship at Hoylake as part of what the R&A described as a “robust” plan to counter sabotage attempts.
Shortly before the disruption, an unlicensed drone went up above the course,  prompting Merseyside Police to swoop to arrest its suspected pilot at a nearby location.

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/formula-1/20.title: Brad Pitt swaggers onto Silverstone grid with Verstappen and Hamilton  – but stunt double speeds off
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/formula-1/20.subtitle: Some fans at British Grand Prix believed Hollywood star, who is filming a new F1 movie, was behind the wheel when race began
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/formula-1/20.text:
He swaggered on to Silverstone’s grid and shook hands with Max Verstappen as the British Grand Prix became a Hollywood shoot in one surreal scene.
However, the main moment of movie magic – Brad Pitt zooming off with the real Formula One drivers – turned out to be complete make-believe.
While the real Pitt, 59, joined the likes of Lewis Hamilton on the grid pre-race, a stunt double duped spectators into believing they were watching the world-famous actor behind the wheel.
Talk had been abuzz among racegoers that Pitt’s car had driven off – albeit for only 75 metres – behind the real drivers for the formation lap ahead of the race proper.
The world-famous actor had appeared on the grid pre-race in his overalls, standing alongside drivers for the national anthem and then appearing to walk back to his converted F2 car in 22nd place. Seconds later, his fictional No 7 Apex car roared away shortly after the other cars and across the start line.
However, what most had failed to spot was that Pitt, who drove two hot laps on Saturday, had not walked all the way back to his car’s cockpit. Amid the high stakes of having just one shot to get the scene right and additional fears of a Just Stop Oil protest, the film’s directors were taking no chances.
Instead of Pitt and his co-star Damson Idris featuring behind the wheel, former racers turned stuntmen Craig Dolby and Luciano Bacheta stepped in.
The movie, being made by Apple Original Films and produced by Jerry Bruckheimer Films and Pitt’s Plan B Entertainment, has done its utmost to keep as much of its plot secret while filming at major sporting events at the same time.
They reached agreements with the likes of Sky Sport, who limited any shots of Pitt’s character Sonny Hayes or his fictional Apex car at the back of the grid during live coverage.
Staff and accredited media were also instructed not to look too much at the actors to ensure shots felt as authentic as possible for the makers of Top Gun: Maverick.
What the directors could not account for, however, was the reaction of some spectators in the pre-race grid walk to one of the most famous faces in Hollywood.
One child, presumably a relative of one of the celebrities or business figures allowed privileged access, failed to contain his amazement, covering his mouth and pointing at the star as he appeared alongside the drivers for the anthem.
Pitt had also waved to the crowd after he was cheered and shook hands with runaway championship leader Verstappen and former champion-turned-pundit Jenson Button.
Even drivers had described events as bizarre. “I think it’s one of those when you see a worldwide superstar for the first time, it’s quite surreal,” said Mercedes’ George Russell of Pitt’s appearance.
Verstappen, however, had joked that he had less enthusiasm for the project over the weekend, saying: “I completely can’t be bothered with this.”
Pitt is being closely advised by Versappen’s old rival Hamilton, who has a consultancy producer role on the film.
The actor, meanwhile, told Sky Sports of the film: “What’s amazing about it is that you’ll see the cameras mounted all over the car. The shots - you’ve never G-forces like this, it’s really, really exciting.”

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/world-news/2.text:
Climate activists threw black and yellow paint over a private jet parked at Ibiza Airport on Friday evening, completely obscuring its windscreen.
Protesters from Futuro Vegetal and Extinction Rebellion said three of its members entered the airport’s runway on Friday morning, dousing a jet in paint and forcing the runway to close for several hours.
Photos show the protesters using fire extinguishers to spray the jet, which reportedly cost over £10 million, with black, yellow and pink paint before standing on its wings and lighting flares.
“Your luxury = our climate crisis,” a banner held by one of the protesters reads.
On Twitter, Futuro Vegetal said: “This is how one of the activists expressed herself in today’s action with Extinction Rebellion Ibiza. “The jets of the rich are a luxury we cannot afford.
“Eat the rich. Take action”
